title: AES-128 K8 stage: four more K9 bytes (conditional) (Giraud, AES2004 proceedings published 2005)

display.name: K8 stage: four more K9 bytes (conditional)

target.description: Full AES-128; use K8-tail recovery and Eq.(28) to identify K9[8..11], given the already recovered K9[12..15].

setting.key_relation: One fixed secret AES master key; no related-key oracle.
setting.key_population: Keys of the stated AES implementation without a weak-key restriction; fault protections are outside the model.
setting.plaintext_model: Repeat encryptions of the same plaintext under the same key; retain its correct ciphertext as a reference. Counts of faulty ciphertexts exclude that reusable reference unless explicitly stated otherwise.

fault_model.target: K8[12..15] after correct round-8 use, before online generation of K9.
fault_model.granularity: One initially affected byte, followed by propagation through the key schedule or AES rounds.
fault_model.timing: After K8 is correctly used and before generating K9.
fault_model.location: Choose the K8 tail bytes; the stated stage budget combines the special and ordinary byte cases.
fault_model.value_control: The byte difference is unknown; its value may be inferred or guessed from correct/faulty outputs. Eq19 enumerates unknown fault masks, not key candidates:107–146 possibilities, mean126.50390625 over uniform output deltas; the source≈127 remains an approximation.
fault_model.sample_pairing: Every faulty output is matched to the same fixed-input correct reference; useful faults, random-location ciphertexts and physical executions have distinct accounting.

assumptions: A round key is used correctly for encryption and then faulted before generating the next round key. The implementation expands keys on the fly.
The reported outcome and data budget use the paper's candidate-filtering model; no numerical whole-key success rate is inferred from a byte-level statistic.
This is a conditional stage, not an attack starting with no known subkey material.

prior_key_knowledge.material: K9[12..15] from the first key-schedule stage.
prior_key_knowledge.cost_accounting: The listed stage budget excludes acquisition of this prior subkey material; the upstream recovery must be costed separately.

time.note: No numerical whole-endpoint runtime is reported for this version and endpoint.

data.note: Chosen-byte stage-2 budget, excluding the 8 stage-1 outputs. It does not assert a numeric joint four-byte success probability.

memory.note: The article describes counters or candidate lists without a numerical peak-memory budget.

preprocessing.note: No separate reusable preprocessing-time budget is reported. The Appendix A 8×2^8 equation tests per useful output are a component count, not a complete attack cost.

success.description: No numerical whole-output recovery probability is supplied for this exact endpoint and sample budget. The19-fault K8 stage uses13 exceptional-byte plus six ordinary-byte faults. Its exceptional-byte99% experiment does not quantify the joint four-byte stage.

review.scope: Exact-edition endpoint-specific success audit. Theoretical deterministic guarantees require the stated ideal model; local filters, characteristic products, expected counts and physical acquisition are separate. Costs, targets, settings, existing conflicts and full-audit gates are unchanged.

components.description: Section4.2 Equations19/22/27: with correct prior K9 tail and an accepted effective modeled fault, the actual K8 byte satisfies the enumerated equations. This is candidate retention, not uniqueness after two faults or a completed stage.

Section4.2 simulation: K8[12] is identified in99% of cases after13 useful faults (90% after10). This is one exceptional byte conditional on correct K9 prerequisites; no trial denominator is supplied. It is not the simultaneous success of the three ordinary bytes or downstream M8 completion.

limitations: Useful faulty ciphertext counts do not automatically include ineffective physical injections or calibration attempts.
The article does not supply a measured success frequency, runtime or peak memory for every target and parameter choice.

The exactly-one-zero output test can reject valid tail faults with extra zero differences. Independent finite valid-key cases find94 such rejections among16320 tail faults;48960 sampled non-tail faults give no false accepts, not a universal soundness proof. Keep reported useful-sample versus acquisition counts distinct.

Even with correct K9[12..15], two distinct accepted whole-byte faults need not uniquely identify an ordinary K8 byte in Eq27. A valid AES128 master2ed1746d5ef479cfcc00003c10989845 and plaintext620b86738303a9696fde8432799d46ed give M8=K8=0 and correct K9=78636363 repeated four times. For each j13/14/15, faults01/bc pass the exactly-one-zero postselection, correctly decode e/f by Eq22, and leave the same four Eq27 candidates{00,01,bc,bd}. This is an independent local limitation, not an inherited incorrect-K9 prerequisite. Retain the source2/19/31 sample estimates and unknown joint success; no replacement mean or whole-attack failure is inferred. The special-byte12 simulation frequencies are not refuted by this witness.
